There is limited evidence regarding the optimal timing for discontinuing aspirin therapy aimed at preventing pre-eclampsia. 3. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) acknowledges that in certain settings, the use of aspirin near the time of delivery may prevent the administration of epidural or spinal anesthesia. 4. The GDG recommends that aspirin discontinuation should align with local practices concerning the use of anticoagulants during pregnancy. 5. The GDG emphasizes the need for further research to better understand the balance between the benefits of pre-eclampsia prevention and the potential risks of postpartum and neuraxial hemorrhage associated with late-pregnancy use of low-dose aspirin. 6. This recommendation replaces Recommendation No. 8 from the 2011 WHO guidelines on the prevention and treatment of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia. 7. In 2017, an estimated 295,000 women and adolescent girls died due to complications related to pregnancy and childbirth, with 99% of these deaths occurring in low-resource settings. 8. Hemorrhage, hypertensive disorders, and sepsis account for over half of all maternal deaths globally. 9. Improving the quality of maternal healthcare is essential to achieving the health targets outlined in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the WHO’s Thirteenth General Programme of Work, particularly in achieving universal health coverage. 10. International human rights law obligates states to ensure that women and adolescent girls survive pregnancy and childbirth as part of their sexual and reproductive health rights and their right to live a life of dignity. 11. The WHO envisions a world where every pregnant woman and newborn receives quality care throughout pregnancy, childbirth, and the postnatal period. 12. Evidence suggests that effective interventions exist at reasonable costs to prevent or treat nearly all life-threatening maternal complications. 13. Approximately two-thirds of the global maternal and neonatal disease burden could be alleviated through the optimal adaptation and implementation of existing research findings. 14. To provide high-quality care, healthcare providers at all levels, especially in lowand middle-income countries, must have access to appropriate medicines, health products, and training in relevant medical procedures. 15. Healthcare providers, managers, policymakers, and other stakeholders require up-to-date, evidence-based recommendations to guide clinical policies and practices, optimize care quality, and improve healthcare outcomes. 16. Preventing morbidity and mortality during pregnancy and childbirth can reduce profound global inequities in maternal and perinatal health. 17. Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are a significant cause of severe morbidity, long-term disability, and death among mothers and their babies, accounting for approximately 14% of all maternal deaths worldwide. 18. Among hypertensive disorders, pre-eclampsia and eclampsia are major contributors to maternal and perinatal mortality and morbidity. 19. Most deaths due to pre-eclampsia and eclampsia can be prevented through timely and effective care for women presenting with these complications. 20. The Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) prioritized updating the WHO recommendations on aspirin use for pre-eclampsia prevention in response to new evidence. 21. WHO has established a systematic process for prioritizing and updating maternal and perinatal health recommendations, overseen by an international group of independent experts known as the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG). 22. Recommendations are prioritized for updating based on changes or uncertainties in evidence regarding benefits, harms, values, acceptability, feasibility, equity, resource use, cost-effectiveness, or implementation factors. 23. The updated recommendations were developed following the standards and procedures outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development, including evidence synthesis, GRADE methodology, and input from a Guideline Development Group (GDG) of international experts and stakeholders. 24. The primary aim of these recommendations is to improve the quality of care and outcomes for women giving birth, particularly concerning the prevention and management of pre-eclampsia. 25. The target audience includes healthcare professionals responsible for developing national and local guidelines, as well as those providing care during labor and childbirth, such as midwives, nurses, general practitioners, and obstetricians. 26. These recommendations are also relevant to managers of maternal and child health programs, policymakers, educational institutions, and pregnant women themselves. 27. The recommendations were framed using the Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome (PICO) format to address specific clinical questions. 28. The population affected by these recommendations includes all pregnant women. 29. The guideline development process involved identifying priority questions and outcomes, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, and evaluation. 30. In 2019, updating recommendations on antiplatelet agents for pre-eclampsia prevention was identified as a high priority due to new evidence. 31. The process involved six main groups of experts and stakeholders, including the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG), WHO Steering Group, Guideline Development Group (GDG), Evidence Synthesis Group (ESG), external partners, and an External Review Group (ERG). 32. The WHO Steering Group managed the process of updating the recommendations, including drafting key questions, engaging systematic review teams, and organizing GDG meetings. 33. The GDG, composed of 16 external experts and stakeholders, reviewed evidence, formulated recommendations, and reached unanimous consensus on the final document. 34. The Evidence Synthesis Group (ESG) conducted systematic reviews, appraised evidence, and developed Evidence to Decision (EtD) frameworks. 35. Evidence on values, acceptability, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness was obtained through mixed-methods reviews and literature analysis. 36. External partners and observers, including representatives from USAID, ICM, FIGO, and the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, participated in GDG meetings to support guideline dissemination and implementation. 37. The External Review Group (ERG) reviewed the final document for factual accuracy, clarity, and contextual relevance, ensuring that decision-making processes incorporated the values and preferences of affected individuals and healthcare professionals. 38. Priority outcomes for the updated recommendations included maternal well-being and satisfaction, ensuring a woman-centered approach to care.
